chapter_summary:
Bringing non-player characters (NPCs) to life in your game involves designing and scripting their behaviors, a field known as Artificial Intelligence (AI). In Unreal Engine, the brain of an AI character is typically an `AI Controller`. Just as a `Player Controller` processes input from a human player, an `AI Controller` processes information from the game world and dictates the actions of its controlled Pawn or Character. When you place an AI character (like an enemy or a friendly NPC) into your level, it needs an `AI Controller` assigned to it. You can create a custom `AI Controller` Blueprint by inheriting from `AIController` or `A_AIController` and then assign this custom controller class in your AI character's Blueprint details panel. The `AI Controller` is where you'll typically house the logic for decision-making, pathfinding requests, and reacting to perceived stimuli, keeping the AI character's Pawn Blueprint focused on animation, mesh, and physical properties. A common mistake is trying to put all AI logic directly into the AI character's Pawn Blueprint, which can lead to messy and less reusable code. Separating concerns between the Pawn (what it is) and the Controller (how it thinks) is a best practice.

One of the fundamental aspects of AI is perception – how an AI character "sees" or "hears" the world around it. Unreal Engine provides the `AIPerceptionComponent` to manage this. This component can be added to your AI Controller or AI character Blueprint. It allows you to configure various "senses" such as `Sight`, `Hearing`, `Damage`, `Team`, and `Prediction`. For basic AI, `Sight` and `Hearing` are most commonly used. When you add an `AIPerceptionComponent`, you'll configure its properties: for `Sight`, this includes `Sight Radius`, `Lose Sight Radius`, `Peripheral Vision Angle`, and `Detection by Affiliation` (e.g., detect enemies, friends, or neutral). For `Hearing`, you'll set `Hearing Range`. The `AIPerceptionComponent` then continuously "perceives" the world and generates `OnTargetPerceptionUpdated` events when it detects or loses track of an actor. This event provides information about the perceived actor, whether it was successfully sensed, and what sense detected it. This event is the gateway to making your AI react to the player or other NPCs. For example, if the player enters the AI's `Sight Radius` and is within its `Peripheral Vision Angle`, the `OnTargetPerceptionUpdated` event will fire, indicating the player has been sensed.

With perception in place, you can start scripting basic AI movement. A common pattern for non-aggressive AI is patrolling. This involves moving between a series of predefined waypoints. You can achieve this by creating an array of `TargetPoint` actors in your level, or simply storing a list of `Vector` locations in your AI Controller. The AI would then use the `Move To Location or Actor` Blueprint node to navigate to the first waypoint. Upon reaching it (indicated by the `OnRequestFinished` event of the `Move To Location or Actor` node), it would then select the next waypoint in the sequence and move there, looping through the array. For aggressive AI, the behavior shifts to chasing. When the `AIPerceptionComponent` detects the player, the AI Controller would then call `Move To Location or Actor`, targeting the player character directly. It's crucial to ensure your level has a `NavMesh Bounds Volume` properly built and covering the areas where your AI needs to move. Without a `NavMesh`, AI characters cannot pathfind and will simply stand still or attempt to move in a straight line, often getting stuck. Common mistakes include forgetting to build the `NavMesh` (press 'P' in the editor to visualize it) or having gaps in it.

To manage these different behaviors (Idle, Patrol, Chase), AI often uses a concept called a "state machine." A state machine defines a finite number of states an AI can be in, and transitions between these states based on certain conditions. In Blueprints, you can implement a simple state machine using `Enum` variables and `Switch on Enum` nodes. For example, you might define an `E_AI_State` enum with values like `Idle`, `Patrol`, `Chase`, `Attack`. When the game starts, the AI might be in the `Idle` state. If the `AIPerceptionComponent` senses the player, the AI's state could transition from `Idle` to `Chase`. When the player leaves the AI's sight, the state might transition from `Chase` back to `Patrol` or `Idle`. Each state would then have its own specific logic: the `Patrol` state calls `Move To Location or Actor` to waypoints, while the `Chase` state continuously updates its target to the player's location. This modular approach makes it easier to manage complex AI behaviors and debug issues, as you can clearly see which state the AI is currently in and what conditions trigger state changes. It's important to design clear transition rules to avoid AI getting stuck in undesired states or flickering between states.

Debugging AI can be challenging, especially with movement and perception. Always use the built-in debug tools. For `AIPerceptionComponent`, you can visualize its sight and hearing ranges in the editor by selecting the component. For navigation, press 'P' to visualize the `NavMesh`. During runtime, you can use the `ShowDebug AI` console command (or `ShowDebug AI Perception`, `ShowDebug AI Navigation`) to see what the AI perceives, its current path, and its active behavior. This is invaluable for understanding why an AI isn't moving or reacting as expected. Another common issue is AI characters getting stuck on obstacles. Ensure your character's collision settings are appropriate and that the `NavMesh` accurately reflects the walkable areas. Sometimes, increasing the `Agent Radius` in the `NavMesh` settings can help prevent AI from trying to path through areas too narrow for their collision capsule.

screens.title: Designing & Scripting Basic AI Behavior
screens.subtitle: How AI Controllers, perception, movement, and state machines create responsive NPCs

narration.text: In this lesson we focus on building basic AI behavior in Unreal using Blueprints. You will learn why an AI Controller acts as the brain separate from the Pawn, how to give an AI eyes and ears with the AIPerceptionComponent, and how to make characters patrol and chase using AI Move To and a simple enum-based state machine. We’ll also cover the practical necessities for navigation: NavMesh Bounds Volume and common debugging steps when AI does not move or perceive correctly. The patterns you learn here keep logic reusable and easier to debug: controllers make decisions, pawns handle visuals and collision. A concrete example we'll use throughout is a simple enemy that patrols between two TargetPoint waypoints and switches to chase when it senses the player. Finally, I’ll show common mistakes such as placing logic in the Pawn instead of the Controller or forgetting to build the NavMesh, and how to check perception affiliation or blocked sight traces. By the end you’ll understand the building blocks needed to script reliable, testable AI behaviors.

keyIdea.title: Core idea
keyIdea.text: Separate thinking (AI Controller) from being (Pawn); use AIPerception for senses; use NavMesh and AI Move To for movement; manage behaviors with a simple state machine.

Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › Designing & Scripting Basic AI Behavior

Designing & Scripting Basic AI Behavior

Learn the practical blueprint patterns for perception, movement, and simple state machines that drive NPCs in your levels.

In this lesson
AI Controller role, perception, movement, and state machine implementation.
Coming up
Hands-on patrol & chase activity using TargetPoints and AI Move To.
Why it matters
Clean separation of logic helps reuse and makes debugging perception and pathfinding easier.
AI System Overview
Controller → Perception → Movement → State
AI Controller
Holds decision logic, binds to AIPerceptionComponent, issues Move To requests, and manages state variables like current waypoint index.
AIPerception
Configurable senses such as Sight and Hearing. Fires OnTargetPerceptionUpdated when actors appear or disappear from senses.
Movement
AI Move To uses the NavMesh to pathfind to a location or actor. Requires NavMesh Bounds Volume to be built and cover travel areas.
State Machine
Use an Enum (Idle, Patrol, Chase) and Switch on Enum to organize behavior and transitions cleanly.
Explore Key Topics
AI Controller — brain separated from Pawn
Perception — sight & hearing senses
Patrol & Chase — Move To and NavMesh

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: What you'll be able to do after this chapter

narration.text: These objectives map to practical Blueprints you will build. First, you will explain the role of AI Controllers and how they differ from Player Controllers: controllers separate decision logic from visuals and collision. That distinction prevents mixing input handling with AI decision code. Second, you will implement basic perception using AIPerceptionComponent for sight and hearing, learning to configure sight radius, peripheral angle, and detection by affiliation so your AI senses the player reliably. Third, you will script movement behaviors such as patrolling between waypoints and chasing a perceived target, using AI Move To and NavMesh-aware navigation. Finally, you will design a simple enum-based state machine (Idle, Patrol, Chase) and debug common navigation and perception errors. Each objective includes a small mnemonic and a verified competency milestone so you can confirm the skill: assign a controller, configure senses, script Move To responses, and switch states on perception events. These skills together let you create a patrol-and-chase enemy and diagnose why it may not see or move as expected.

Four Testable Checks
  1. Controller assignment: Confirm BP_EnemyAIController is set on BP_EnemyAI and BeginPlay events run in the controller.
  2. Perception events: Bind OnTargetPerceptionUpdated and validate sensing when player enters Sight Radius and peripheral angle.

Debug tools

Common pitfalls
Putting AI logic in the Pawn instead of the Controller, incorrect affiliation settings, or an incomplete NavMesh are frequent causes of nonresponsive AI.

screens.title: AI Controller: the AI's brain
screens.subtitle: Why controllers own decision logic and pawns own visuals and collision

narration.text: An AI Controller is the decision-making authority for an AI character. Think of the Controller as the brain: it interprets world data, decides goals, and issues movement and action requests. The Pawn or Character is the body: it holds meshes, collision, and animation. This separation matters because it keeps behavior reusable and reduces coupling. For example, a single controller Blueprint can drive different pawn meshes or characters without duplicating AI logic. In practice you create a custom AI Controller by inheriting from AIController (BP_EnemyAIController) and assign it to the Pawn in the Pawn’s details panel. A common mistake is placing pathfinding, perception binding, or state variables inside the Pawn Blueprint. That keeps behavior tied to a single mesh instance and makes debugging harder. Instead, put perception components, state enums, patrol arrays, and movement requests on the Controller. When testing, verify the controller receives BeginPlay and that movement logs and perception callbacks are logged from the controller. Understanding this separation is the first step to building modular and maintainable AI. AI Controller: the AI's brain means keep decision logic in ai controller; keep animation, mesh, and collision in pawn to enable reuse and clearer debugging.. In practical terms, why controllers own decision logic and pawns own visuals and collision. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Separation of concerns
keyIdea.text: Keep decision logic in AI Controller; keep animation, mesh, and collision in Pawn to enable reuse and clearer debugging.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › AI Controller: the AI's brain
Definition
The AI Controller interprets perception, makes decisions, requests movement, and manages state variables separate from the Pawn.
• Place perception bindings and state enums on the Controller for reuse.
• Use controller BeginPlay to initialize patrol routines and timers.
• Keep Pawn focused on visuals: meshes, animation, and collision only.
Concrete example
Create BP_EnemyAIController and assign it in BP_EnemyAI details. Put StartPatrol and perception binding in the controller so different pawns can share the same behavior.
Common mistake
Putting pathfinding and OnTargetPerceptionUpdated logic in the Pawn makes the behavior harder to reuse across different enemy types.
Role diagram (card-first)
Controller
  • Bind AIPerceptionComponent events
  • Manage E_AI_State and patrol index
  • Call AI Move To and Stop Movement
Pawn / Character
  • Static Mesh / Skeletal Mesh
  • Capsule Collision and animation
  • Not responsible for perception bindings
Takeaway
Controllers make logic reusable and testing easier.
Pro tip
Use log prints on controller events to confirm behavior is executed from the controller, not the pawn.
Watch out
Avoid duplicating perception bindings in both controller and pawn; it creates confusing callbacks.

screens.title: AIPerceptionComponent & Senses
screens.subtitle: Configuring Sight and Hearing and reacting to OnTargetPerceptionUpdated

narration.text: AIPerceptionComponent is the system that lets AI 'sense' the world. It supports multiple senses; for basic AI we focus on Sight and Hearing. When you add an AIPerceptionComponent, configure Sight Radius, Lose Sight Radius, Peripheral Vision Angle, and Detection by Affiliation. Peripheral Vision Angle defines the cone of vision, so even if the player is within the sight radius they won’t be sensed unless they fall inside that cone. Hearing requires a hearing range and listens for noisey events. The component continuously evaluates stimuli and fires OnTargetPerceptionUpdated when an actor enters or leaves perception. That event reports whether the actor was successfully sensed and which sense triggered it. A practical pattern is to bind this event in the AI Controller BeginPlay, check whether the actor is the player character and whether Successfully Sensed is true, then set your AI state to Chase and call AI Move To with the actor as a target. A common misconception is that increasing Sight Radius alone guarantees detection; you must also check affiliation and line-of-sight blocking by geometry. Use the editor's perception debug visualization and the ShowDebug AI Perception console command during runtime to inspect traces and blocked visibility.

keyIdea.title: Perception pattern
keyIdea.text: Bind OnTargetPerceptionUpdated in the controller, check sense and affiliation, then update state and movement based on Successfully Sensed.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › AIPerceptionComponent & Senses
Senses to configure
Sight
  • Set Sight Radius and Lose Sight Radius
  • Set Peripheral Vision Angle (cone)
  • Set Detection by Affiliation (Enemies/Friendlies/Neutrals)
Hearing
  • Set Hearing Range
  • Generate noise events from player or AI
  • Can trigger chase without visual contact if configured
Event pattern
Bind OnTargetPerceptionUpdated in BeginPlay of the AI Controller. The event yields the perceived actor, whether sensing succeeded, and the sense type. Use that to set E_AI_State and call AI Move To when necessary.
Quick example
When Successfully Sensed is true and the actor is the player, set CurrentAIState to Chase and call AI Move To targeting the player's actor. If perception reports false, revert state to Patrol and resume patrolling.
Misconception check
Do not assume Sight Radius implies line-of-sight: blocked collision or wrong trace channels can prevent detection. Also confirm affiliation settings so the player can actually be detected.
Key Takeaway

AIPerceptionComponent centralizes senses; its events are the gateway to state changes like Chase or Patrol.

screens.title: Patrolling: waypoints and AI Move To
screens.subtitle: Implementing a looping patrol using TargetPoints and move requests

narration.text: Patrolling is a simple but common AI behavior where an AI moves between defined waypoints. Start by placing TargetPoint actors in your level and adding them to a PatrolWaypoints array on your AI Controller. Keep an integer CurrentWaypointIndex initialized to zero. Create a StartPatrol custom event that gets the actor at CurrentWaypointIndex and calls AI Move To with that waypoint's location. When the Move To request succeeds (On Success), increment CurrentWaypointIndex with wrap-around so it loops, then call StartPatrol again after a short delay. This pattern is robust and easy to debug: you can add log prints at each waypoint arrival and visually inspect the NavMesh to ensure the path is valid. Be careful about hardcoding vectors instead of using TargetPoints, because actors placed in the editor are easier to adjust during iteration. Also ensure your NavMesh Bounds Volume covers the entire patrol route—without it the AI will not pathfind and may attempt straight-line movement that gets it stuck. Use delays and On Success events rather than tight loops so the AI has time to reach the waypoint and animations can synchronise with movement.

keyIdea.title: Patrol loop
keyIdea.text: Use a patrol array of TargetPoints, AI Move To, On Success event, and indexed wrap-around logic to implement a looping patrol.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › Patrolling: waypoints and AI Move To
Top/bottom split — patrol process
Steps
  1. Place TargetPoint actors (Waypoint_A, Waypoint_B) in the level.
  2. Add PatrolWaypoints array to BP_EnemyAIController and populate with the waypoints.
  3. Create CurrentWaypointIndex integer and StartPatrol custom event.
  4. In StartPatrol, call AI Move To using the waypoint's actor location; on success increment index and delay before next StartPatrol.
Example
CurrentWaypointIndex = 0, PatrolWaypoints = [Waypoint_A, Waypoint_B]. StartPatrol moves to Waypoint_A, On Success sets index to 1, delay, then moves to Waypoint_B, then wraps to 0.
Key Takeaway

Use TargetPoints and On Success events for reliable patrol loops that work with NavMesh pathfinding.

Common mistake

Forgetting to build or cover the patrol area with a NavMesh causes AI Move To to fail or produce straight-line movement.

Implementation cards
PatrolWaypoints: Array<Actor> — fill in editor or populate dynamically.
StartPatrol: Get(PatrolWaypoints, CurrentWaypointIndex) → AI Move To → On Success increment index and Delay(1s) then StartPatrol.
Wrap-around: if index >= length then set to 0.

screens.title: Chasing: reacting to perception
screens.subtitle: Switching to Chase state and continuously updating target location

narration.text: Chasing is the behavior where an AI abandons patrol to move toward a perceived actor, typically the player. The typical implementation begins in the OnTargetPerceptionUpdated event bound on the AIPerceptionComponent in the AI Controller. If Successfully Sensed is true and the actor is recognized as the player, set CurrentAIState to Chase and call AI Move To with the actor as the target. To keep chasing a moving player, you should periodically retrigger AI Move To with the player's current location—do this with a retriggerable delay or timer so the path updates frequently without flooding path requests. When perception reports the player is no longer sensed, set CurrentAIState back to Patrol, call Stop Movement, and call StartPatrol to resume the waypoint loop. Watch out for flickering states: ensure your transition rules include small delays or checks so the AI doesn't rapidly flip between Chase and Patrol because of momentary perception loss. Also confirm that AI Move To is used with an actor target rather than a static vector when you want the path to follow a moving target. This pattern gives responsive chasing while remaining robust on complex NavMeshes.

keyIdea.title: Chase behavior
keyIdea.text: On successful perception of the player, set state to Chase and repeatedly AI Move To the player's actor; revert to Patrol on loss of perception.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › Chasing: reacting to perception
Chase control flow
• Bind OnTargetPerceptionUpdated in the controller. If Successfully Sensed and actor is player then set state to Chase.
• Call AI Move To targeting the perceived actor. Use actor-targeted Move To so the path updates as the player moves.
• Use a retriggerable Delay or Timer to update the Move To target every 0.3–0.6 seconds while in Chase state.
• When perception reports false, Stop Movement, set state to Patrol, and call StartPatrol.
Misconception check
Don’t assume one Move To call will track a moving target; schedule regular Move To updates or use actor-targeted Move To with periodic retriggering to keep the AI following smoothly.
Example
On perception true: Set CurrentAIState = Chase → AI Move To(Target: Player) → On Success Delay(0.5) then AI Move To again while state = Chase.
Key Takeaway

Retrigger Move To while chasing to follow a moving target and use Stop Movement plus StartPatrol when the target is lost.

screens.title: State Machine Design with Enums
screens.subtitle: Organize Idle, Patrol, and Chase logic using E_AI_State

narration.text: A simple state machine is an effective way to keep AI behavior organized. Define an E_AI_State enum with values such as Idle, Patrol, and Chase. Store a CurrentAIState variable on the AI Controller and use a Switch on Enum node to select which branch of logic runs. On BeginPlay set the default state to Patrol and call StartPatrol. When perception senses the player, set the state to Chase and enter the chase logic branch that retriggers AI Move To. If the player is lost, set the state back to Patrol and resume waypoint logic. Each state should be responsible for its own actions so transitions are clear and straightforward. For example, Patrol calls StartPatrol and Chase manages continuous Move To calls. This modular design prevents logic from mixing and makes it simpler to debug which state the AI is in. A common problem is missing a fallback path—ensure there is clear handling for unexpected cases, such as what to do if a Move To fails. Also add small timers or cooldowns when transitioning to prevent rapid state flicker from noisy perception events.

keyIdea.title: State machine
keyIdea.text: Use an enum and Switch on Enum to separate behavior into explicit states with clear entry and exit rules, reducing complexity and debugging time.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › State Machine Design with Enums
Hierarchy
• Create E_AI_State enum with Idle, Patrol, Chase (and optionally Attack).
• Add CurrentAIState variable to the AI Controller and default it to Patrol.
• Use Switch on Enum where behavior decisions are evaluated, and route execution to the appropriate logic branch.
• Keep state-specific functions isolated: StartPatrol for Patrol, ChaseLoop for Chase, etc.
Example transitions
• BeginPlay: CurrentAIState = Patrol → StartPatrol()
• OnTargetPerceptionUpdated (sensed): CurrentAIState = Chase → Start chase retrigger loop
• OnTargetPerceptionUpdated (lost): CurrentAIState = Patrol → Stop Movement → StartPatrol()
Misconception
Avoid putting multiple behaviors in a single state. Each state should be responsible for clear actions and transitions so you can inspect and test them individually.
Key Takeaway

Enums plus Switch on Enum create readable state machines. Design explicit entry and exit rules to avoid flicker between states.

screens.title: Move To Location or Actor & NavMesh
screens.subtitle: How AI Move To uses the NavMesh and why NavMesh Bounds Volume is essential

narration.text: AI Move To is the Blueprint node that requests pathfinding for an AI Controller. It can take either an actor or a location as a target. When used with an actor, AI Move To will attempt to path to the actor’s current position; when used with a location, it pathfinds to that fixed position. Both rely on the navigation mesh (NavMesh) generated by NavMesh Bounds Volumes. If a NavMesh doesn't cover the area, AI Move To cannot compute a path and the pawn will either not move or attempt direct straight-line movement that causes getting stuck or clipping through geometry. A key setup step is placing NavMesh Bounds Volume to cover all travel areas and building the NavMesh; press 'P' in the editor to visualize the walkable surfaces. During runtime, ShowDebug AI Navigation displays the current path. If AI gets stuck often check collision capsule size against NavMesh agent settings; increasing Agent Radius or adjusting step heights may solve narrow passage issues. In sum, always confirm NavMesh coverage and alignment with your AI’s physical parameters before troubleshooting pathfinding behavior. Move To Location or Actor & NavMesh means ai move to requires a built navmesh that covers movement areas; without it, pathfinding fails and ai movement becomes unreliable.. In practical terms, how ai move to uses the navmesh and why navmesh bounds volume is essential. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Navigation dependency
keyIdea.text: AI Move To requires a built NavMesh that covers movement areas; without it, pathfinding fails and AI movement becomes unreliable.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › Move To Location or Actor & NavMesh
Architecture
• AI Move To(Target Actor) updates path as the actor moves; use retriggering to refresh frequently.
• AI Move To(Target Location) moves to a fixed vector; useful for waypoints or patrol points.
• NavMesh Bounds Volume defines where the NavMesh will be generated; press 'P' to visualize it in the editor.
Debug checklist
  • Is NavMesh present and covering the route? (Press 'P')
  • Does agent radius and step height match the pawn collision?
  • Use ShowDebug AI Navigation to inspect path and blocked nodes during runtime.
Common fix
Add or resize NavMesh Bounds Volume and rebuild the NavMesh. Verify the walkable area includes your TargetPoints and patrol paths.
Symptom
AI stands still or walks straight through obstacles—likely missing NavMesh or incorrect agent settings.

screens.title: Controller Event Graph — Patrol & Perception (Starter Template)
screens.subtitle: A minimal event graph outline for BeginPlay, perception binding, StartPatrol, and perception handling

narration.text: Seeing the flow in code form helps you implement the controller logic. The starter template describes BeginPlay calling StartPatrol, binding OnTargetPerceptionUpdated, and handling perception events to toggle Chase and Patrol. Implement StartPatrol to retrieve the current waypoint from the PatrolWaypoints array, call AI Move To, and on success increment the index and call StartPatrol again after a delay. In OnTargetPerceptionUpdated, check Successfully Sensed and whether the actor is the player character. On true, set CurrentAIState to Chase and call AI Move To towards the perceived actor. On false, set state back to Patrol, call Stop Movement and StartPatrol. When translating this pseudocode to Blueprints, use custom events, Bind Event to OnTargetPerceptionUpdated, and the AI Move To node. This structure divides responsibilities and makes it easier to log and debug when a specific branch does not execute as expected. Use timers or retriggerable delays for continuous chase updates. Controller Event Graph — Patrol & Perception (Starter Template) means beginplay -> startpatrol; ontargetperceptionupdated toggles chase or patrol; startpatrol uses ai move to with on success loop.. In practical terms, a minimal event graph outline for beginplay, perception binding, startpatrol, and perception handling. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Event graph pattern
keyIdea.text: BeginPlay -> StartPatrol; OnTargetPerceptionUpdated toggles Chase or Patrol; StartPatrol uses AI Move To with On Success loop.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › Controller Event Graph — Starter Template
Starter pseudocode (Blueprint flow description)
[Event BeginPlay]
    -> [StartPatrol]

[AIPerceptionComponent OnTargetPerceptionUpdated]
    -> [Branch] (Condition: Successfully Sensed && Is Player Character)
        [True]
            -> [Set CurrentAIState (Chase)]
            -> [AI Move To (Target: perceived actor)]
            -> [On Success] -> [Delay (0.5s)] -> [AI Move To (Target: perceived actor)] (loop while in Chase)
        [False] (Player Lost)
            -> [Set CurrentAIState (Patrol)]
            -> [Stop Movement (self)]
            -> [StartPatrol]

[Custom Event StartPatrol]
    -> [Get (PatrolWaypoints) at CurrentWaypointIndex]
    -> [AI Move To (Target: waypoint location)]
    -> [On Success]
        -> [Increment CurrentWaypointIndex (with wrap-around)]
        -> [Delay (1.0s)]
        -> [StartPatrol]
Copy this structure into your AI Controller event graph using custom events, Bind Event to OnTargetPerceptionUpdated, and AI Move To nodes. Add log prints to trace the execution path during testing.
Key Takeaway

Translate this template into Blueprints: BeginPlay sets patrol, perception toggles chase, patrol loops on success.

Pro tip
Use a Retriggerable Delay node in the Chase loop so you can cancel or restart the retrigger easily when state changes.

screens.title: Debugging Perception & Navigation
screens.subtitle: Use editor visualization and debug commands to find why AI doesn’t sense or move

narration.text: Debugging AI involves inspecting what the system thinks and what the navigation system provides. If an AI with AIPerceptionComponent configured for Sight doesn’t react even when the player stands directly ahead, two common causes are affiliation settings and blocked visibility traces. First, check Detection by Affiliation: ensure the component is set to detect the player's affiliation—Enemies, Friendlies, or Neutrals—depending on how team settings are defined. Second, verify line-of-sight isn't blocked by invisible collision or misconfigured trace channels. In the editor, select the AIPerceptionComponent and enable its visualization, then during runtime run ShowDebug AI Perception to see the actual traces. For navigation problems where AI gets stuck or walks through walls, the typical missing element is a correctly placed NavMesh Bounds Volume. Press 'P' to view the NavMesh in the editor and ensure the patrol area is covered. Also inspect Agent Radius and collision capsule size; mismatches cause the AI to choose invalid paths or try to squeeze through narrow gaps. Use ShowDebug AI Navigation to see the active path and nodes. These visual tools are invaluable and usually reveal configuration errors quickly.

keyIdea.title: Debug toolkit
keyIdea.text: ShowDebug AI Perception and ShowDebug AI Navigation plus editor visualizations are essential first steps when AI doesn’t perceive or navigate correctly.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › Debugging Perception & Navigation
Perception checks
  • Confirm Detection by Affiliation includes the player.
  • Verify Peripheral Vision Angle so the player is inside the vision cone.
  • Use ShowDebug AI Perception to see traces and which sense fired during runtime.
Visibility issue
An invisible blocking volume or wrong collision channel can prevent sight traces; inspect trace hits in the debug view to find the blocker.
Navigation checks
  • Press 'P' to visualize NavMesh; ensure patrol and chase areas are covered.
  • Use ShowDebug AI Navigation to inspect current path and look for invalid nodes.
  • Check Agent Radius and capsule collision to avoid narrow passage issues.
Common fix
Resize NavMesh Bounds Volume or rebuild NavMesh so AI has valid pathing surfaces for its patrol and chase routes.

screens.title: Activity: Build a Patrolling & Chasing Enemy
screens.subtitle: Step-by-step checklist for the in-editor exercise

narration.text: This hands-on activity walks you through creating a patrolling enemy that chases the player when seen. First, create BP_EnemyAI derived from Character and add a mesh and Capsule Collision. In its details set AI Controller Class to BP_EnemyAIController which you will create next. Add an AIPerceptionComponent to BP_EnemyAI and configure Sight: Sight Radius 1500, Lose Sight Radius 2000, Peripheral Vision Angle 60, and set Detection by Affiliation to detect the Player. Next, create BP_EnemyAIController derived from AIController. In its Event Graph get the AIPerceptionComponent from the controlled pawn and bind OnTargetPerceptionUpdated. Add an Array variable PatrolWaypoints and an Integer CurrentWaypointIndex initialized to 0. Implement StartPatrol to AI Move To the waypoint at the current index, and on success increment index (wrap around) and call StartPatrol after Delay(1.0). In OnTargetPerceptionUpdated set CurrentAIState to Chase on successful sensing of the player and call AI Move To targeting the player; on losing sense set state to Patrol, Stop Movement and StartPatrol. Finally add a NavMesh Bounds Volume, cover the patrol path and press 'P' to verify. Run and use ShowDebug commands to iterate until the AI patrols and chases reliably.

keyIdea.title: Activity checklist
keyIdea.text: Implement BP_EnemyAI and BP_EnemyAIController, configure perception, add waypoints and patrol logic, bind perception events for chase, and ensure NavMesh coverage.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › Activity: Build a Patrolling & Chasing Enemy
Step-by-step
  1. Create BP_EnemyAI (Character): add mesh and capsule, set AI Controller Class to BP_EnemyAIController.
  2. Add AIPerceptionComponent to BP_EnemyAI and configure Sight (1500, 2000, 60) and affiliation detection.
  3. Create BP_EnemyAIController (AIController) and in BeginPlay bind OnTargetPerceptionUpdated from controlled pawn's perception component.
  4. Add PatrolWaypoints array and CurrentWaypointIndex; create StartPatrol custom event that AI Move To waypoint, On Success increment and loop with Delay(1s).
  5. In perception handler set state to Chase and call AI Move To actor while sensed; on loss set to Patrol, Stop Movement, and StartPatrol.
  6. Add NavMesh Bounds Volume covering route and press 'P' to visualize. Use ShowDebug AI Perception and ShowDebug AI Navigation while testing.
Expected result
The AI patrols between waypoints and switches to chase the player when sensed, then returns to patrol when the player is lost.
Test tips
Place waypoints clearly visible in the level, then toggle NavMesh visualization and debug perception traces during runtime to iterate quickly.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.subtitle: Three essential ideas from this chapter

narration.text: Here are the core concepts to carry forward. First, the AI Controller is the 'brain' and should own decision-making, perception bindings, and movement requests; keep Pawn Blueprints focused on visuals and collision. Second, AIPerceptionComponent centralizes senses like Sight and Hearing. Configure radii, peripheral angles, and detection by affiliation and bind OnTargetPerceptionUpdated to react when actors are sensed or lost. Third, navigation depends on a valid NavMesh generated within NavMesh Bounds Volume; without it AI Move To cannot pathfind reliably. Use enums and a simple state machine—Idle, Patrol, Chase—to keep behavior organized, and rely on editor visualizations and ShowDebug commands to diagnose perception and navigation problems. These ideas together let you build modular, debuggable AI that patrols, chases, and returns to patrol in a predictable way. Use the hands-on activity as your verification loop to ensure each concept works in your project.

keyIdea.title: Essentials
keyIdea.text: Controller = brain; AIPerception = senses; NavMesh = required for AI Move To pathfinding.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › Key Concepts
AI Controller
Owns decision-making, perception, path requests and state variables.
AIPerceptionComponent
Provides senses (Sight, Hearing) and fires OnTargetPerceptionUpdated events.
NavMesh / AI Move To
AI Move To uses the NavMesh generated by NavMesh Bounds Volume for reliable pathfinding.
Summary
Combine controllers, perception, state machines, and a proper NavMesh to create patrol-and-chase enemies you can iterate and debug quickly.

screens.title: Key Concepts — Quick Reference
screens.subtitle: Three short reminders before you code

narration.text: A quick reference to keep at hand: 1) Assign a custom AI Controller and put perception and state logic there; that keeps Pawns reusable. 2) Configure AIPerceptionComponent carefully: sight radius, lose radius, peripheral angle, and detection by affiliation determine when OnTargetPerceptionUpdated fires. 3) Ensure the NavMesh Bounds Volume covers all paths the AI will take; press 'P' to check and use ShowDebug commands to view runtime perception traces and navigation paths. With these three checks in place you can build a patrol-and-chase enemy and avoid the most common causes of nonresponsive AI. Key Concepts — Quick Reference means controller holds logic; aiperception manages sensing; navmesh enables pathfinding—verify these first when troubleshooting ai.. In practical terms, three short reminders before you code. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Quick reference
keyIdea.text: Controller holds logic; AIPerception manages sensing; NavMesh enables pathfinding—verify these first when troubleshooting AI.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › Key Concepts — Quick Reference
1. Controller owns logic
Place perception bindings, patrol arrays, and state variables on the controller for reuse and clarity.
2. Configure perception
Set Sight Radius, Lose Sight Radius, Peripheral Angle, and affiliations to ensure the player can be detected.
3. Verify NavMesh
NavMesh Bounds Volume and agent settings must match the pawn so AI Move To can find valid paths.
Final reminder
Use the provided hands-on checklist to implement and then use ShowDebug commands to iterate until patrol and chase are reliable.
